claim: deepPCA quantified the effects of >120,000 pairs of point mutations on the formation of the AP-1 transcription factor complex between the products of the FOS and JUN proto-oncogenes.
source: Here, by developing a new sequencing-based protein interaction assay – deepPCA – we quantified the effects of >120,000 pairs of point mutations on the formation of the AP-1 transcription factor complex between the products of the FOS and JUN proto-oncogenes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of mutation pairs quantified and the proteins studied.

claim: Genetic interactions are abundant both in cis (within one protein) and trans (between the two molecules).
source: Genetic interactions are abundant both in cis (within one protein) and trans (between the two molecules) and consist of two classes – interactions driven by thermodynamics that can be predicted using a three-parameter global model, and structural interactions between proximally located residues.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the study.

claim: Genetic interactions consist of two classes: interactions driven by thermodynamics that can be predicted using a three-parameter global model, and structural interactions between proximally located residues.
source: Genetic interactions are abundant both in cis (within one protein) and trans (between the two molecules) and consist of two classes – interactions driven by thermodynamics that can be predicted using a three-parameter global model, and structural interactions between proximally located residues.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the two classes of genetic interactions identified in the study.

claim: Most genetic variation consists of point mutations not deletions or null alleles.
source: However, gene deletions are rare in nature – most genetic variation consists of point mutations not deletions or null alleles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Point mutations can have very diverse and difficult to predict effects.
source: Point mutations can have very diverse and difficult to predict effects (Shendure and Akey, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There has been no systematic effort to map how point mutations in two genes combine together to alter biological functions prior to this study.
source: To date, however, there has been no systematic effort to map how point mutations in two genes combine together to alter biological functions.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Mutations affecting protein-protein interactions lead to disease, to functional innovations, and are subject to selection.
source: Mutations affecting PPIs lead to disease, to functional innovations, and hence are subject to selection (Diss et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Pairs of mutations in two physically interacting proteins can have non-additive outcomes.
source: It has long been appreciated that pairs of mutations in two physically interacting proteins can have non-additive outcomes (Horovitz, 1996; Lehner, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Fos and Jun interact through their leucine zipper domains that consist of five heptad repeats.
source: Fos and Jun interact through their leucine zipper domains that consist of five heptad repeats (Figure 1A); this interaction has been previously extensively investigated (Mason et al., 2006; Ransone et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, with citations to prior work.

claim: PPI scores measured by deepPCA are highly reproducible between biological replicates with mean Pearson correlation R = 0.95.
source: PPI scores measured by deepPCA are highly reproducible between biological replicates (mean Pearson correlation R = 0.95 between the three pairs of replicates, n = 108,840 mutation combinations, Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The correlation value is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the data.

claim: deepPCA measurements correlate with mutation effects tested individually (R = 0.95 for 14 variants).
source: and also with mutation effects tested individually (R = 0.95 for 14 variants chosen randomly, Figure 1D).
evidence: The correlation with individual tests is stated and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Reliable measurements were obtained for 607 and 608 of the 608 possible single amino acid changes within the targeted regions of Fos and Jun, respectively.
source: We obtained reliable (input reads > 10 and output reads > 0; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; see Materials and methods) measurements for 607 and 608 of the 608 (32 positions x 19 substitutions) possible single amino acid (aa) changes within the targeted regions of Fos and Jun, respectively.
evidence: The number of measurements obtained is explicitly stated.

claim: Approximately 20% and 15% of substitutions in Fos and Jun, respectively, are severely detrimental for the interaction.
source: The PPI scores for single amino acid changes in both proteins show a bimodal distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), with ~20% and 15% of substitutions severely detrimental for the interaction and significantly different from the wild-type (PPI score ≤ 0.64, FDR < 0.05, one sample t-test against a mean of 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The percentages are stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: 25 and 10 amino acid changes in Fos and Jun, respectively, strengthen the interaction.
source: However, the individual substitutions altered the interaction across the entire dynamic range, with 25 and 10 aa changes in each protein strengthening the interaction (PPI score > 1.04, FDR < 0.05, average SEM of these 35 variants = 0.0054; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The specific numbers of strengthening mutations are stated.

claim: Mutations in the hydrophobic core of the interaction interface (heptad positions a and d) are most detrimental.
source: Mutations in the hydrophobic core of the interaction interface (heptad positions a and d) are most detrimental, followed by mutations at salt-bridge positions (positions e and g, Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Mutations at salt-bridge positions (positions e and g) are the second most detrimental after hydrophobic core mutations.
source: Mutations in the hydrophobic core of the interaction interface (heptad positions a and d) are most detrimental, followed by mutations at salt-bridge positions (positions e and g, Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A-B.

claim: Mutations in the hydrophilic far side of the zipper (positions b, c and f) were generally of small effect.
source: Mutations in the hydrophilic far side of the zipper (positions b, c and f) were generally of small effect (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Changes in physico-chemical properties of amino acids provide good prediction of mutation effects, with percentage of variance explained from 35% to 98% across Fos and Jun positions.
source: Changes in the physico-chemical properties of the amino acids (hydrophobicity, charge, α-helical stability etc, see Supplementary file 2) provide good prediction of the mutation effects (percentage of variance explained from 35% to 98% across Fos and Jun positions), with properties related to α-helical stability most informative for predicting single mutation outcomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The variance explained range is stated in the text.

claim: Properties related to α-helical stability are most informative for predicting single mutation outcomes.
source: Changes in the physico-chemical properties of the amino acids (hydrophobicity, charge, α-helical stability etc, see Supplementary file 2) provide good prediction of the mutation effects (percentage of variance explained from 35% to 98% across Fos and Jun positions), with properties related to α-helical stability most informative for predicting single mutation outcomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Identical substitutions in the same positions in Fos and Jun often had similar effects.
source: Identical substitutions in the same positions in Fos and Jun often had similar effects.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Mutations in one protein that disrupted the interaction (PPI scores < 0.64) were very likely to disrupt the interaction when made in the other protein (odds ratio = 31.6, p<2.2×10−16).
source: For instance, mutations in one protein that disrupted the interaction (PPI scores < 0.64) were also very likely to disrupt the interaction when made in the other protein (odds ratio = 31.6, p<2.2×10−16, Fisher's exact test; Figure 2D).
evidence: The odds ratio and p-value are stated, indicating statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Near neutral or strengthening mutations (PPI scores > 0.96) in one protein were more likely to have a similar effect in the other protein (odds ratio = 7.3, p < 2.2×10−16).
source: Near neutral or strengthening mutations (PPI scores > 0.96) in one protein were also more likely to have a similar effect in the other one (odds ratio = 7.3, p < 2.2×10−16, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The odds ratio and p-value are stated.

claim: A substantial number of substitutions (n = 381 out of 581) had effects that differed between Fos and Jun (FDR < 0.05).
source: However, a substantial number of substitutions had effects that differed between the two proteins (n = 381 out of 581, FDR < 0.05, paired t-test between the three replicate measurements in Fos and Jun), underlining the importance the structural context in which they occur.
evidence: The specific number and statistical test are stated.

claim: Data was obtained for 107,625 of the 369,664 possible double mutants in trans.
source: Considering pairs of substitutions in the two proteins, we obtained data for 107,625 of the 369,664 possible double mutants (input read count above 10 and output read count above 0, Supplementary file 1, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The number of double mutants measured is explicitly stated.

claim: The double mutant PPI scores show a bimodal distribution with proportionally more severely detrimental (~26%) and fewer near-neutral outcomes (~21%) than for the single mutants.
source: The double mutant PPI scores also show a bimodal distribution, but with proportionally more severely detrimental (~26%) and fewer near-neutral outcomes (~21%) than for the single mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: The percentages are stated and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The outcome of double mutations was well predicted by multiplying the PPI scores of the constitutive single mutants (percentage of variance explained of 85–86% in all three replicates).
source: The outcome of the double mutations was well predicted by multiplying the PPI scores of the constitutive single mutants (percentage of variance explained of 85–86% in all three replicates, Figure 3B), that is, by assuming no genetic interaction between mutations.
evidence: The variance explained is stated and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 16,394 cases of negative genetic interactions and 11,653 cases of positive genetic interactions were detected at a 20% FDR.
source: Negative and positive genetic interactions (16,394 and 11,653 cases, respectively, at a 20% FDR, one-sample t-test) thus represent double mutants with lower or higher interaction strength than expected, respectively.
evidence: The specific numbers of genetic interactions are stated.

claim: Combining two mutants that both moderately reduce PPI strength is likely to result in a negative genetic interaction.
source: Combining two mutants that both moderately reduce PPI strength is likely to result in a negative genetic interaction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This pattern is stated and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Positive genetic interactions are generally detected between two mutations that greatly weaken the interaction and often when combining strength-increasing and strength-decreasing mutations.
source: Positive genetic interactions are, however, generally detected between two mutations that greatly weaken the interaction and also often when combining strength-increasing and strength-decreasing mutations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This pattern is stated and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The thermodynamic model has only three free parameters representing the total concentration of each protein and the background growth in the PCA selection.
source: This model has only three free parameters that need to be fitted from the data, representing the total concentration of each protein and the background growth in the PCA selection (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The number and meaning of parameters are explicitly stated.

claim: The thermodynamic model provides very good prediction of how mutations in the two proteins combine together (percentage of variance explained of 89–90% in all three replicates).
source: Fitting the three parameters from the data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B) reveals that the model provides very good prediction of how mutations in the two proteins combine together (percentage of variance explained of 89–90% in all three replicates, n = 107,618 mutation combinations, Figure 3E).
evidence: The variance explained is stated and shown in figures.

claim: More cases of strong negative (1711, 1.6%) than positive (883, 0.82%) genetic interactions were observed (absolute score > 0.1, FDR = 0.2).
source: We observed more cases of strong negative (1711, 1.6%) than positive (883, 0.82%) genetic interactions (absolute score > 0.1, FDR = 0.2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: The specific numbers and percentages are stated.

claim: Positive genetic interactions are concentrated between positions close in the sequence of heptad positions.
source: These strong interactions are enriched between particular Fos and Jun residues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with positive genetic interactions concentrated between positions close in the sequence of heptad positions (along the diagonal of the matrix in Figure 4A)
evidence: This pattern is stated and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Negative genetic interactions are more spread-out in the structure and less enriched between specific pairs of positions.
source: and negative genetic interactions more spread-out in the structure and less enriched between specific pairs of positions (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This pattern is stated and shown in figures.

claim: Both directions of genetic interaction are enriched between residues at the interface of the PPI and between residues close in space.
source: Both directions of interaction are enriched between residues at the interface of the PPI and between residues close in space (Figure 4C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), with this stronger for positive than for negative interactions.
evidence: The enrichment patterns are stated and shown in figures.

claim: Positive genetic interactions are particularly enriched between contacting residues, identifying 'lock and key' specificity residues.
source: Positive interactions are therefore particularly enriched between contacting residues, identifying 'lock and key' specificity residues (Horovitz, 1996).
evidence: This interpretation is stated with a citation to prior work on the concept.

claim: Data was obtained for 17,688 double amino acid changes within Fos alone (99% of cis double mutant combinations reachable through combinations of single nucleotide changes).
source: In addition to combining pairs of mutations in the two different proteins, we also quantified the effects of 17,688 double amino acid changes within Fos alone (99% of cis double mutant combinations reachable through combinations of single nucleotide changes; for all comparisons between the trans and cis libraries below, we only consider mutants reachable by single nucleotide changes in both libraries; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 3 and 4).
evidence: The number of cis double mutants is explicitly stated.

claim: PPI scores for single mutants correlate very well between the cis and trans libraries (R = 0.96).
source: The PPI scores for single mutants correlate very well between the two libraries (R = 0.96, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), further validating the reproducibility of the deepPCA method.
evidence: The correlation value is stated and shown in a figure.

claim: There is a good correlation (R = 0.77) between the PPI scores of cis and trans double mutants consisting of exactly the same pairs of substitutions at the same positions.
source: There is a good correlation between the PPI scores of cis and trans double mutants consisting of exactly the same pairs of substitutions at the same positions (R = 0.77, n = 5451 identical double mutants quantified in cis and trans, Figure 5B).
evidence: The correlation value and number of mutants are stated and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Two mutations within Fos are more likely to increase the strength of the PPI than one mutation in Fos combined with a second mutation in Jun (5.2% vs 3.4%, p < 10−3).
source: This revealed that, even when controlling for single mutant effect sizes, two mutations within Fos are more likely to increase the strength of the PPI than one mutation in Fos combined with a second mutation in Jun (p < 10−3 over 1000 sub-samplings, 5.2% vs 3.4%, respectively, for PPI scores > 1.04, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The percentages and p-value are stated.

claim: Two mutations in Fos are slightly less likely to destroy the PPI than a trans mutation combination (25.5% vs 27.8%, p < 10−3 for PPI scores < 0.64).
source: Two mutations in Fos are slightly less likely to destroy the PPI than a trans mutation combination (25.5% vs 27.8%, respectively, p < 10−3 for PPI scores < 0.64, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The percentages and p-value are stated.

claim: Two mutations in Fos have slightly more intermediate negative effects than trans combinations (39.4% vs 35.3%, p < 10−3, for PPI scores between 0.64 and 0.92).
source: but have slightly more intermediate negative effects (p < 10−3, 39.4% vs 35.3%, respectively, for PPI scores between 0.64 and 0.92, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: The percentages and p-value are stated.

claim: Leucine zippers, including Fos and Jun, fold upon binding.
source: Because leucine zippers, including Fos and Jun, fold upon binding (Patel et al., 1990; Thompson et al., 1993), the same thermodynamic model based on a two-state equilibrium between the two unfolded proteins and the complex can describe how mutations combine in cis as well as in trans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The thermodynamic model fitted on trans double mutants gave very good prediction of the cis library data (percentage of variance explained of 82–83% for cis vs. 90–91% for trans combinations).
source: We tested how well the thermodynamic model with parameters fitted on the trans double mutants predicted the cis library data and found that it gave very good prediction (percentage of variance explained of 82–83% for cis vs. 90–91% for trans combinations, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The variance explained values are stated.

claim: Fitting the thermodynamic model on the cis double mutants gave very good prediction of the trans library data (percentage of variance explained of 84% for cis and 90% for trans).
source: Similarly, fitting the thermodynamic model on the cis double mutants gave very good prediction of the trans library data (percentage of variance explained of 84% for cis and 90% for trans, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The variance explained values are stated.

claim: Structural genetic interactions explain more of the variance in double mutant PPI scores when mutations are combined in cis than in trans.
source: Interestingly, structural genetic interactions explain more of the variance in double mutant PPI scores when mutations are combined in cis than in trans (Figure 5D).
evidence: This comparison is stated and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both positive and negative structural genetic interactions are more abundant in cis than in trans (1493 vs. 835 true cases of positive and 1319 vs. 1128 true cases of negative genetic interactions).
source: Indeed, both positive and negative structural genetic interactions (genetic interactions not accounted for by the thermodynamic model; Supplementary files 3 and 4) are more abundant in cis than in trans (1493 vs. 835 true cases of positive and 1319 vs. 1128 true cases of negative genetic interactions in cis and trans, respectively, at p < 0.031, one sample t-test, FDR < 0.15 and 0.2; Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 9).
evidence: The specific numbers are stated.

claim: There are more contacts between positions within FOS (1040 cis mutant pairs) than across the interface (518 trans mutant pairs at positions within 5 Å of each other).
source: This higher prevalence of genetic interactions in cis can potentially be explained by a higher number of contacts between positions within FOS than across the interface (1040 cis vs. 518 trans mutants pairs at positions within 5 Å of each other), supporting our previous result that proximity is a major determinant of genetic interactions both in cis and trans in a PPI interface.
evidence: The specific numbers of contacts are stated.

claim: Physical interactions in the cell generate two distinct types of genetic interaction: interactions due to the sigmoidal relationship between the concentration of a protein complex and the free energy of an interaction, and specific structural interactions.
source: Our data reveal that physical interactions in the cell generate two distinct types of genetic interaction: interactions due to the sigmoidal relationship between the concentration of a protein complex and the free energy of an interaction (Figure 3) and specific, structural interactions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion from the study.

claim: A three parameter thermodynamic model accounts for ~90% of the variance in the dataset of >120,000 genotypes.
source: This type of genetic interaction is cumulative and easily predictable, for example a three parameter thermodynamic model accounts for ~90% of the variance in our dataset of >120,000 genotypes.
evidence: The variance explained is stated as a summary of the results.

claim: deepPCA is limited to small domains in its current form because of the limit in amplicon size for paired-end sequencing.
source: In its current form, deepPCA is limited to small domains because of the limit in the amplicon size for paired-end sequencing.
evidence: This limitation is explicitly stated.

claim: The use of barcodes would allow the deepPCA assay to be applied to longer proteins.
source: However, the use of barcodes (Hiatt et al., 2010) would allow the assay to be applied to longer proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future improvement with a citation.

claim: Additional non-linearities occur in the folding of individual proteins or RNAs ('threshold robustness').
source: Additional non-linearities occur in the folding of individual proteins or RNAs ('threshold robustness') (Bershtein et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2014; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009), in saturating enzyme flux (Kacser and Burns, 1973; Stiffler et al., 2015), and in regulatory dynamics (Gjuvsland et al., 2007; Omholt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Non-linearities occur in saturating enzyme flux.
source: Additional non-linearities occur in the folding of individual proteins or RNAs ('threshold robustness') (Bershtein et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2014; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009), in saturating enzyme flux (Kacser and Burns, 1973; Stiffler et al., 2015), and in regulatory dynamics (Gjuvsland et al., 2007; Omholt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Non-linearities occur in regulatory dynamics.
source: Additional non-linearities occur in the folding of individual proteins or RNAs ('threshold robustness') (Bershtein et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2014; Tokuriki and Tawfik, 2009), in saturating enzyme flux (Kacser and Burns, 1973; Stiffler et al., 2015), and in regulatory dynamics (Gjuvsland et al., 2007; Omholt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Whether a second mutation happens in cis or in trans can impact an evolutionary outcome.
source: This results in a different distribution of double mutant outcomes when combining mutations in cis and trans. Whether a second mutation happens in cis or in trans can therefore impact an evolutionary outcome.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed differences.

claim: Deep sequencing data is available at GEO with accession number GSE102901.
source: Deep sequencing data is available at GEO with accession number GSE102901 (reviewer token: yvgbkwqajvypvah).
evidence: The data availability statement is explicit.

claim: All experiments were performed in BY4742 yeast strain.
source: All experiments were performed in BY4742 (MATα his3Δ1 leu2Δ0 lys2Δ0 ura3Δ0).
evidence: The yeast strain used is explicitly stated.

claim: All experiments were performed in triplicates starting from the transformation of the variant libraries into yeast.
source: All experiments were performed in triplicates starting from the transformation of the variant libraries into yeast.
evidence: The experimental design is explicitly stated.

claim: The Fos and Jun basic leucine zipper domains correspond to residues 135 to 199 and 250 to 314, respectively.
source: FOS and JUN basic leucine zipper domains, as defined by SMART (Letunic et al., 2015), were amplified from human cDNA provided by Juan Valcarcel using primer pairs OGD098-OGD110 and OGD113-OGD125, respectively. These fragments correspond to residues 135 to 199 and 250 to 314, respectively.
evidence: The residue ranges are explicitly stated.

claim: The transformation resulted in 19.88 × 10^6, 19.32 × 10^6 and 16.52 × 10^6 transformants for replicates 1, 2 and 3 of the trans library.
source: This transformation resulted in 19.88 × 106, 19.32 × 106 and 16.52 × 106 transformants for replicates 1, 2 and 3.
evidence: The transformation efficiency numbers are explicitly stated.

claim: A total of 245,676,608 read pairs were obtained from the sequencing lane for the trans library.
source: A total of 245,676,608 read pairs were obtained from the lane.
evidence: The sequencing output is explicitly stated.

claim: Approximately 30% of sequencing reads corresponded to adaptor sequences and had to be discarded.
source: However, ~30% corresponded to adaptor sequences and had to be discarded.
evidence: The percentage of discarded reads is stated.

claim: The per base error probability in sequencing was estimated to be 0.0019 for the forward read and 0.0058 for the reverse read.
source: We estimate the probability of a base to be wrongly called to be 0.0019 for the forward read and 0.0058 for the reverse read, averaged across the six samples (three replicates inputs and outputs).
evidence: The error rates are explicitly stated.

claim: The transformation resulted in 1.17 × 10^7, 9.6 × 10^6 and 1.09 × 10^7 transformants for replicates 1, 2 and 3 of the cis library.
source: This transformation resulted in 1.17 × 107, 9.6 × 106 and 1.09 × 107 transformants for replicates 1, 2 and 3, respectively.
evidence: The transformation efficiency numbers are explicitly stated.

claim: A total of 262,393,254 read pairs were obtained from the sequencing lane for the cis library.
source: A total of 262,393,254 read pairs were obtained from the lane, with ~ 12% adapter sequences.
evidence: The sequencing output is explicitly stated.

claim: Approximately 12% of sequencing reads for the cis library were adapter sequences.
source: A total of 262,393,254 read pairs were obtained from the lane, with ~ 12% adapter sequences.
evidence: The percentage of adapter sequences is stated.
